analysis.one_liner: Overhauls the credit report dispute process, adds a free appeal right, and bans deceptive credit-monitoring marketing.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 32-26, but it was never brought to the House floor for a vote before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the Fair Credit Reporting Act to make it easier for people to fix errors on their credit reports: credit bureaus would have to run real investigations with trained, US-based staff, forward all of a consumer's documents to the company that reported the data, and let consumers appeal for free within 120 days. It also bans the "free trial" credit-monitoring subscriptions that quietly turn into paid services, requires warnings before negative information is reported, mandates access in the 10 most common languages and for people with vision or hearing impairments, and directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write accuracy rules and register credit reporting agencies.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 200 million adults whose credit files are held by Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian, especially the share with errors — a Federal Trade Commission study cited in the bill found 26 percent of surveyed consumers had at least one potentially material error on their report. Errors on credit reports can cost people a job, an apartment, or a mortgage, so faster, more substantive dispute resolution, a free appeal, and the ability to get a court order forcing fixes would mainly help ordinary borrowers, renters, and job seekers. Nonnative English speakers and people with vision or hearing impairments would gain mandated access to dispute materials in their language and accessible formats.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers disputing errors on credit reports

how_it_helps.text: Forces credit bureaus to conduct genuine reinvestigations of disputed items — trained staff located in the US, an independent review that considers all documents the consumer submits, and direct authority for dispute staff to delete or correct information that cannot be verified, rather than rubber-stamping whatever the furnisher says.

Creates a new consumer right to appeal, free of charge within 120 days, the results of a dispute — reviewed by employees who did not handle the original case and who cannot be paid or promoted based on how many appeals they process quickly.

Strips credit bureaus and data furnishers of the power to dismiss resubmitted disputes as 'frivolous or irrelevant,' a discretion the bill's findings say consumers found most frustrating, and requires creditors, lenders, and debt collectors to keep records as long as the negative information can stay on a report.

Bans automatic renewals for promotional credit monitoring and credit score products and prohibits misleading marketing — codifying practices the CFPB had already ordered TransUnion, Equifax, and Experian to stop in 2017 consent orders that cost them tens of millions in restitution and penalties.
Gives courts explicit authority to order injunctive relief, so a consumer can get a court to compel a bureau to fix unlawful practices rather than only collect money damages after the harm is done.

Requires dispute information to be available in the 10 most commonly spoken languages in the US and in formats accessible to people with vision or hearing impairments, and lets consumers shop for mortgage and other loan rates without the comparison shopping itself damaging their credit standing.

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies (chiefly Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian) and the companies that furnish data — banks, credit card issuers, and debt collectors — would bear the compliance costs: staffing and training for substantive reinvestigations and appeals, record retention, warning notices before reporting negative information, translated materials, and a new nationwide registry. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through fees or prices, and the bill takes effect only two years after enactment, with CFPB rulemaking taking up to two more years, so relief would be slow.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, banks, and debt collectors

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on a handful of large bureaus and thousands of lenders and debt collectors, who could pass some of those costs to consumers through higher fees or prices.

Requiring a written warning 90 days before reporting negative information (and a follow-up notice within 5 business days afterward) creates a real risk that some lenders respond by furnishing less data at all, which would thin the credit files of people trying to build a credit history.

Relief is slow by design: the bill takes effect two years after enactment, and the CFPB has up to two years to issue implementing rules, so consumers would see no benefit quickly even if it had become law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and broad: nearly every adult has a credit file, errors are common — the FTC study cited in the bill found 26 percent of participants had a potentially material error — and the current dispute system, which the bill's findings describe as quota-driven and reliant on rubber-stamp verification, demonstrably fails people. The costs are real but concentrated on three giant bureaus and large furnishers, and the strongest honest objection (notice requirements thinning credit files) is speculative. On balance the bill was designed to fix a system that imposes much larger costs on consumers than the compliance burden would impose on the industry, though its two-year effective date would have delayed any benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it 32-26 and it was placed on the House calendar in December 2019, but House leadership never scheduled it for a floor vote, and it died when the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alma Adams introduced the bill in July 2019 with no cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
Two days after introduction, the committee marked up the bill and voted 32-26 to order it reported with amendments.
On December 23, 2019, the committee formally reported the amended bill (H. Rept. 116-363) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting House floor action.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a floor vote in the House and never moved in the Senate, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies like Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian, along with the banks and debt collectors that furnish data to them, are better off because the bill died: they avoided new investigation, appeal, recordkeeping, registry, and marketing restrictions. The 26 committee members who voted no also never had to face a recorded floor vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was the committee's 32-26 markup vote, and the bill drew zero Republican cosponsors in a House with 231 Democrats and 197 Republicans, so its support was almost entirely Democratic.

industries.note: The bill strips their discretion to dismiss disputes as frivolous, requires US-based trained staff and independent reinvestigations, gives dispute staff direct power to delete unverifiable data, bans quota-based incentives, adds a registry, and restricts how they sell credit scores and monitoring directly to consumers. Their business model of processing disputes hastily and selling subscriptions to consumers is directly targeted.

Furnishers would have to keep records as long as negative information can stay on a report, investigate disputes independently while considering all consumer documents, handle free appeals, and warn customers 90 days before reporting negative information. These duties raise their cost of reporting data and of defending what they report.

industries.industry: Credit monitoring and credit score subscription sellers
industries.note: The bill bans automatic renewals for promotional credit reporting and scoring products and prohibits misleading marketing, targeting the 'free' or '$1' trials that auto-convert into paid subscriptions — the exact practices that cost TransUnion, Equifax, and Experian tens of millions in CFPB restitution and penalties in 2017.
